36.outcome: The pond freezes from the surface under the chosen heat rule and later melts. Total occupied water/ice volume is tracked.
36.why: We already move water and transfer temperature. Now ask a concrete question: what should happen when the pond crosses zero? A colour change alone would not create an ice surface that supports a structure. The material identity has to change, but the world must still contain the same occupied volume. This lesson turns that requirement into one small, reversible state transition.

sections.title: Separate temperature from material
sections.html: Think of a cell as a record containing both material and temperature. Two water cells may have different temperatures while sharing one material definition. Temperature determines whether the conversion is eligible; the material determines movement and support afterward. Do not encode “cold water” as a colour-only flag and expect the physics to infer that it became a solid. The conversion must explicitly replace Water with Ice. The renderer then reads that state rather than deciding it.

sections.title: Choose the boundary, including equality
sections.html: The design says water below 0°C freezes and ice above 0°C melts. Therefore exactly zero does neither in this simple model. Write those inequalities before coding; changing < to <= changes the rule. A real physical phase-change model would account for latent heat and other details, but that is not what this game currently specifies. We are implementing the visible approximation and naming it honestly, then testing its boundary values.

sections.title: Transition once, then clear state deliberately
sections.html: A conversion is an event, not a loop that repeatedly rewrites a cell. Read the old material and temperature, choose at most one replacement, then return. When porting into the packed Cell record, specify which flags survive. A water-flow marker should not accidentally make fresh ice move again, and a rooted plant flag should never appear on it. Preserve temperature unless the approved thermal rule says otherwise. Preserve or transform moisture according to its meaning; do not blindly reconstruct the default painted cell.

sections.title: From one cell to a pond surface
sections.html: The helper proves thresholds and reversibility, not surface-first freezing. That larger behavior comes from exposure plus heat exchange: the upper water touches cold air, cools, becomes ice, and then conducts toward deeper water. Build a three-row pond fixture with cold air above and warm water below. Track the first converted row by tick and compare it with the ten-second deadline. If every row freezes simultaneously, look for a rule rewriting the entire pond to ambient temperature instead of letting heat move.

37.outcome: Warm snow becomes water within ten seconds at 1x. Cold snow remains snow under the fixture, and conversion clears stale attachment or movement flags as specified.
37.why: Snow arrives as loose powder, so it must settle and then become flowing water when warm. If snow is only a weather drawing, a roof never gains weight and melting never feeds a puddle. We already have powder movement and water behavior; the new piece is an explicit bridge between those existing states.

sections.title: Reuse behavior rather than duplicate water
sections.html: Give Snow a powder kind and its own temperature. Before melting, movement follows the light-powder rule, including wind where enabled. After melting, the resulting Water uses the existing liquid rules. There should not be a second “meltwater engine.” This is why material transitions are powerful: a small local state change can reveal behavior already implemented elsewhere. Test the output identity and let the next simulation pass move it according to the documented update marker.

sections.title: Initialize creation paths consistently
sections.html: Painted snow and weather snow originate in different code. The paint path starts at its paint temperature, while weather chooses precipitation from surface ambient conditions. Both must create a valid Snow cell with the right powder flags and no leftover burning/rooted state. Use a named constructor or transition helper for shared invariants. Keep the origin-specific temperature explicit. A test should create snow through each path, warm it, and run the same conversion rule on both.

sections.title: Measure the ten-second promise
sections.html: At a base rate of 20 executed ticks per real second, ten seconds provides 200 ticks at 1x. That is a visibility deadline, not permission to wait exactly 200 ticks. Establish a fixture with snow touching warm air, measure when the first cell changes to water, and check the limit. If the heat model takes longer, tune its approved coefficients rather than secretly accelerating the test clock. Retain a cold control so unconditional melting cannot pass.

sections.title: Decide what a melted cell retains
sections.html: Water should occupy the same grid slot immediately after the change unless movement occurs through the ordinary pass. This keeps volume accounting simple: one Snow cell becomes one Water cell in this abstraction. A snow-specific attachment, wind-delay counter or colour variant must not prevent the new liquid from flowing. For the small lab, store material and temperature only. In the full Cell record, list fields retained, cleared and recomputed so the transition remains deliberate as the engine grows.

38.outcome: Both effects appear within the stated 1x deadline. Counts and energy exceptions are documented instead of hidden.
38.why: The first lava-water contact is a signature cause-and-effect scene for this sandbox. The player should see steam and cooled rock quickly. The mechanism joins existing heat transfer, material conversion and occupancy rules; the challenge is to make that join explicit rather than hide a collection of arbitrary pairwise hacks.

sections.title: Separate transfer from reaction selection
sections.html: First determine whether the cells are neighbours and what heat moves across their shared edge. Then evaluate material transition rules using a clearly defined state: old temperatures or the completed heat-pass temperatures. Choose one pass order and test it. If some rules see old values and others see partially updated values, the first contact may depend on scan direction. The lab isolates reaction selection with already eligible temperatures; it is not a full physically accurate heat solver.

sections.title: Name the special contact policy
sections.html: The design requires basalt at lava-water contact within one second. That is a visible game rule, not a consequence guaranteed by a minimal conductivity equation. Specify whether basalt forms from any contact or only after the lava cools below a threshold, then test that chosen rule. The example below adopts immediate eligible contact as an explicit teaching policy: Water becomes Steam and Lava becomes Basalt. Before production integration, compare that policy to the approved milestone decision.

sections.title: Preserve occupancy and clear stale state
sections.html: Two occupied cells become two occupied cells. The water does not need a free air slot to become Steam because it changes in place; subsequent gas movement finds its path. Lava changes to a supported solid and must enter the support system. Do not place basalt into the water slot while also leaving the lava unchanged unless that is an explicitly budgeted mass source. Record which temperatures and flags result so repeated contact does not emit free extra steam every tick.

sections.title: Turn the deadline into a fixture
sections.html: Place one lava cell next to one water cell, run ordinary simulation ticks, and record first Steam plus first Basalt. At 20 TPS the one-second deadline is 20 ticks at 1x. Compare that with a hot-sand/water fixture, whose maximum is three seconds. A test that merely checks the materials after thousands of ticks misses the actual promise. Keep rendering inspection too: a one-cell Steam change may be technically correct but visually unreadable without movement and colour.

39.outcome: Condensation occurs roughly 40–80 cells above formation when the active region contains that path. Camera clipping is reported separately.
39.why: Previously a camera-relative cloud band made steam condense at different world locations when the observer moved. The fix is not “draw the band higher.” Steam must carry its own temperature and cool through the same local update wherever it exists. The camera chooses whether it is active, not its thermodynamic rule.

sections.title: Store the moving state with the gas
sections.html: A Steam cell contains temperature just like other non-air materials. When movement swaps it with air, that temperature travels with it. Cooling therefore belongs to the cell update, not a screen row. If you leave temperature in the old grid position while moving only the material id, the gas seems to forget its heat and the newly exposed air inherits meaningless state. Move the complete Cell value or explicitly transfer all relevant fields.

sections.title: Tune distance from rate and lifetime
sections.html: Suppose the gas rises two cells per tick. Condensing after about 20–40 ticks gives an undisturbed travel distance around 40–80 cells. A simple lab subtracts a fixed amount of temperature each tick until a threshold is reached. Production cooling toward local ambient may depend on conditions, so “roughly fixed” is a tuning target, not a theorem. Record source temperature, ambient value, rise rule and threshold whenever measuring the distance.

sections.title: Respect obstacles and the active margin
sections.html: A roof can block upward motion while the trapped gas continues cooling. That means condensation may happen close to its source rather than at the open-air target distance, which is sensible for the local rule. If the active boundary absorbs steam first, credit weather humidity according to the design and report it as boundary absorption. Do not pretend an off-screen deletion proves that condensation occurred. The camera-independence test must compare a shared active interior with enough space for the full path.

sections.title: Use a controlled trace before the full scene
sections.html: Start one steam parcel at a known temperature and altitude. Each tick record temperature and altitude; stop on conversion. This gives a table that can be narrated on video: state before, cooling, rise, state after. Repeat with the source translated upward by 100 cells while keeping ambient fixed. The number of updates should stay the same. Then restore ambient altitude dependence and explain any changed result as climate, not camera behavior.

40.outcome: The example needs no unsafe code and preserves the single owner of the buffer. The course’s cross-chunk proof remains a separate requirement.
40.why: Two helpers need to mutate different regions of the same buffer. Borrowing the whole vector twice is not the right interface, even if you know the indices differ. We need an operation that expresses the disjointness in the types. split_at_mut gives a small, concrete example before any threads are involved.

sections.title: Read the compiler question correctly
sections.html: An exclusive mutable reference grants access to the region it describes. If two helpers each receive &mut Vec<T>, both would claim the entire vector while their calls overlap. The compiler cannot infer a hidden promise that one will touch only the left half. Shrink the interface to the memory each helper is allowed to change. A mutable slice describes a contiguous region, and splitting the original slice creates two nonoverlapping regions.

sections.title: A boundary proves disjointness
sections.html: For an array of four elements, splitting at 2 yields indices [0,1] and [2,3]. There is no shared element. The right slice begins at its own local index zero, so right[0] is the original element 2. The original owner still owns the array; the temporary borrows provide controlled access. Once the borrows are no longer used, you may inspect the original array again. You did not clone the storage or create independent copies.

sections.title: Keep the split index valid
sections.html: The ordinary split operation requires the boundary to be at most the slice length. Splitting at zero is valid: the left side is empty. Splitting at length is valid: the right side is empty. A boundary beyond length is an error. Validate any user-derived partition before calling the method, or use an appropriate checked interface available in the chosen toolchain. Do not turn an invalid partition into unsafe pointer arithmetic just to avoid a diagnostic.

sections.title: What this does not prove for chunks
sections.html: Disjoint chunk objects do not automatically imply disjoint simulation footprints. A worker may move a grain into a neighbour, inspect a destination beyond its own object or modify shared metadata. The slices in this lab prove only the allowed writes to the slice itself. Before parallelizing chunks, identify every read and write: cell data, moved markers, dirty rectangles, heightmap changes and event queues. Use the same reasoning at that larger boundary rather than treating this example as a magic threading permission.

41.outcome: Single-threaded and threaded paths share rules. No unsafe shared mutation is introduced to bypass an unproven partition.
41.why: The engine already has a sequential rule set. We want to use more CPU cores only if the measured workload needs them. A correct scheduling design starts by identifying jobs that cannot interfere; creating threads first and hoping the race disappears is not a performance plan.

sections.title: Separate schedule from rule semantics
sections.html: A chunk phase determines which jobs may run together. The same movement and heat helpers should work under a sequential dispatcher and a parallel dispatcher. This gives a reference implementation: if adding threads changes the world hash under identical inputs, dispatch or access is wrong. Avoid copying physics code into two independent implementations just to use threads, because every later fix would need to be kept synchronized.

sections.title: Calculate the complete footprint
sections.html: The proposed four-phase schedule groups chunks by x and y parity. Same-phase chunks are separated, but a job can read and write into a neighbouring chunk. Count the maximum displacement plus every destination/neighbour read. The spec limits moves to 31 cells and adds a one-cell check. That still needs a proof for each actual helper and all metadata. State the intervals and verify their intersection is empty for simultaneous jobs; do not infer safety from chunk centres alone.

sections.title: Use a safe ownership strategy
sections.html: The worked example uses disjoint slices so Rust can enforce exclusive access. Real cross-chunk updates may need a snapshot-read/owned-output strategy, staged boundary commands or another safe partition. A snapshot lets workers read the same old state while they own separate output ranges; the serial merge resolves boundary commands in a fixed order. These alternatives trade memory or merge cost for a simpler proof. Choose from measurements and explicit semantics, not from the desire to silence compiler errors.

sections.title: Budget serial work as well
sections.html: Falling groups, particles and support fills run serially after chunk phases because they can span many chunks. Threads do not accelerate those operations automatically. Record both phase timings and serial tail time in the profiler. A fast parallel cell pass can still produce a slow frame if an explosion triggers hundreds of support searches. Keep a sequential fallback and compare full tick duration, not just the threaded region that looks impressive in isolation.

42.outcome: Tests can force a left or right choice without changing simulation rules. Empty ranges and source state are specified.
42.why: A test needs sand to choose left while production needs a deterministic coordinate-based choice. Changing the simulation every time we test a direction would couple rules to the test harness. A narrow trait makes the choice source replaceable while the movement rule stays the same.

sections.title: Find the variation before inventing an abstraction
sections.html: The varying behavior is “choose one of two valid directions,” not “be any possible material.” Material remains an enum because its alternatives are known and data-oriented. Define a trait only around the operation that needs multiple implementations. This keeps the interface deep enough to hide the source of a choice but small enough that a beginner can read the entire contract. Do not turn every struct into a trait simply because traits exist.

sections.title: Describe the contract in the method
sections.html: The lab trait returns a boolean: true means choose left. A production interface might instead accept a bounded range or a context containing seed, tick and cell position. Whichever shape you choose, document it completely. Does calling the method mutate source state? Does the same context always return the same answer? A deterministic source should not rely on thread arrival order; a scripted test source may intentionally return a fixed answer to expose one branch.

sections.title: Read a generic bound as a requirement
sections.html: In fn direction(source: &impl Choice), the helper can call methods promised by Choice without knowing the concrete source type. The compiler generates suitable code for the implementation used. We do not need trait objects, lifetime annotations or a plugin system for this seam. The useful fact is that one rule works with two sources and its callers supply the behavior explicitly. Keep the example small enough to inspect both implementations beside the rule.

sections.title: Use scripted choices to reveal hidden branches
sections.html: Random integration tests can repeatedly miss a rare left or right path. A scripted source forces the branch now: put stone below a grain, air on the left, a trap on the right, then choose left and inspect the result. The coordinate-hash source is tested separately for repeatability and range. This separation gives two clear failures: movement logic is wrong under a chosen input, or the source does not satisfy its documented contract.

43.outcome: Identical cases match and changed inputs are not accidentally ignored. Camera comparisons are restricted to the scope allowed by boundary effects.
43.why: We now have enough interacting rules that “it looks similar” is not a useful regression check. A deterministic run should reproduce the same complete state under identical inputs and schedule. The important work is defining those inputs before comparing anything.

sections.title: Write the replay envelope
sections.html: The seed describes generated terrain and deterministic choices, but it does not describe where the camera went, which cells were active, what the player painted or how much world time each executed step represented. Record starting state, command sequence with step indices, active-region history and multiplier sequence. If a test omits one of these, it may compare genuinely different simulations and call the difference nondeterminism. Keep the envelope explicit in the fixture rather than scattered through global variables.

sections.title: Compare canonical state, not container accidents
sections.html: A world may store chunks in a hash map whose iteration order is not a public physics contract. For comparison, sort chunk keys, then visit cell fields in a defined order. Exclude irrelevant rendering cache data while including material, temperature, moisture and simulation-relevant flags. A quick hash helps summarize thousands of cells, but when it differs, compare fields to locate the first mismatch. In small tests, direct equality is more informative than a checksum alone.

sections.title: Separate three different claims
sections.html: Repeatability under one thread count, equality across thread counts, and invariance under camera motion are distinct claims. The first catches unrecorded inputs. The second tests dispatch and merge semantics. The third can only be scoped to shared active interior where margin walls/absorption do not influence the result. A camera changes which cells run by design, so unrestricted equality after arbitrary panning is impossible under frozen-off-screen simulation. State the exact comparison region and duration.

sections.title: Make the first divergence easy to find
sections.html: Run both simulations one step at a time and compare after every completed tick while debugging. On mismatch, print tick number, chunk key, local coordinate, old/new fields and the commands applied. Once fixed, retain a compact regression fixture that previously failed. A 10000-tick final hash is useful for the gate, but waiting until the end to learn that something went wrong makes diagnosis unnecessarily expensive. Always report the fixed multiplier and initial seed alongside the result.

44.outcome: A wall burns over time instead of vanishing at ignition. Wet and dry wood fixtures behave differently.
44.why: A burning beam should support its roof while it still exists as wood. Replacing the beam with gas at ignition makes the house collapse in a single update, even if the intended fire should take seconds. The solution is to model burning as state of the fuel, with visible flames as a separate product.

sections.title: Keep identity until fuel is consumed
sections.html: A Wood cell remains Wood while its burning flag is set. Its support and collision rules continue to treat it as rigid. A short-lived timer represents remaining fuel; the heat pass reads its burning temperature policy. When fuel reaches zero, replace the material with Ash or Air according to the chosen rule. That removal is the moment support needs reevaluation. This separates ignition, burning duration and structural failure into events you can observe independently.

sections.title: Treat flames as emitted gas, not the fuel itself
sections.html: A burning cell may emit a Flame into an available neighbouring air slot, preferably upward and biased by wind. Flame has its own brief lifetime and carries heat as it moves. If there is no free slot, the fuel can still burn; failure to draw a new flame should not suspend its timer. Conversely, drawing an orange overlay cannot itself spread heat unless it corresponds to the actual flame/fuel rule. Rendering reads state; it does not manufacture an extra combustion simulation.

sections.title: Choose the order of wetting and burning
sections.html: Rain and water affect whether fuel ignites, how it dries and whether an active fire goes out. Write the tick order explicitly: for example, apply precipitation/wetness before testing ignition, then update burning timers and emissions. Other orders are possible but produce different edge behavior. Test rain arriving on the same tick that dry wood reaches ignition. The game demands wet wood resist and rain stop fire within two seconds; those are interaction tests, not just colour choices.

sections.title: Observe a beam rather than a whole forest first
sections.html: Build a short beam supporting one small roof group. Ignite the centre beam cell and track material, burning flag, timer and support outcome. It should remain rigid during positive fuel and become an ordinary conversion result when consumed. Then run the same fixture wet. This scene is small enough to explain every event on video and strong enough to catch the original instant-collapse bug. Only after it passes should the rule be tested in a hillside fire front.

45.outcome: Wet wood resists ignition and metal can satisfy the documented rust condition. The chosen moisture meaning is recorded in the milestone plan.
45.why: Rain wets metal even though metal does not absorb water into pores. The design already needs moisture to control rust, so “porosity is zero” cannot mean “this surface is forever dry.” Before implementing more reactions we must give that field an unambiguous meaning.

sections.title: Separate two physical ideas in the game model
sections.html: Absorbed moisture is water held by porous material; surface wetness is a film/contact condition. They may share one compact field in this simplified game, but only if the interpretation is documented per material. A metal cell can have zero absorption capacity and still carry a wetness value used by rust and drying. This is a design choice, not a claim that a single u8 is a complete scientific water model. The lesson’s proposed lab separates the quantities so their behavior is visible.

sections.title: Decide whether a drop is consumed
sections.html: For porous soil with spare capacity, a rain hit may raise absorbed moisture and consume a simulated water portion. For nonporous metal, the same hit can set a wetness duration or level while producing runoff. If the hit both fills the cell and creates a full extra water cell without accounting, water has been duplicated. Specify units: one grid water cell and one unit of moisture are not automatically equivalent. Use the game’s approximate humidity budget openly instead of hiding conversion ratios.

sections.title: Make drying conditional on exposure
sections.html: Surface films can dry under warm exposed air while sheltered material dries more slowly. The weather system should pass context—sunlight, ambient, wind, shelter—into a bounded drying rule. Do not make material colour itself the wetness source. A darker swatch is an output of moisture state. Test metal under a roof, metal in rain and porous wood after rain stops, so the chosen semantics demonstrate why a house protects stored materials.

sections.title: Resolve the storage decision before packing
sections.html: The eight-byte Cell layout is a constraint, but it does not justify ambiguous behavior. Options include interpreting moisture as absorbed content for porous cells and wetness for metal; allocating a separate bit/timer; or revising the layout after measurement. Write a small table of what each material reads and writes. The rust rule should consume the documented wetness path, not silently ignore its own prerequisite. Keep this marked as a milestone design proposal until agreed.

46.outcome: Panning across a weather boundary changes conditions smoothly. Returning to the same coordinate/time reproduces baseline values.
46.why: Weather is a property of the world at a time, not a random choice made when the camera enters a chunk. We want two observations of the same place and calendar instant to agree. That requirement leads naturally to a functional baseline plus a small stored record of what the player changed.

sections.title: Choose the independent coordinates
sections.html: Divide horizontal world space into weather columns 512 cells wide. Their centres hold baseline humidity, cover, wind and temperature-offset values derived from seed and world time. The camera coordinate is absent from this function. You can evaluate a far column without running its material cells, which fits frozen off-screen simulation. This is not the same as freezing the climate forever: world time still selects the current baseline when that region is observed again.

sections.title: Interpolate instead of creating a border wall
sections.html: A hard assignment of one weather value per column creates a visible jump at every 512-cell boundary. For a position between neighbouring centres, calculate a fraction from 0 to 1 and blend their values. Humidity and cloud cover can blend directly; wind direction should be represented as a vector or a carefully defined scalar to avoid angular wrap surprises. The lab uses a linear scalar blend so its meaning can be checked before adding seeded noise.

sections.title: Store only deviations that need history
sections.html: A rain-cloud tool or evaporation changes local humidity in a way the baseline function cannot reproduce from seed and time alone. Store that as a delta, then evaluate actual humidity as bounded baseline plus delta. The delta decays toward zero under a documented calendar rule. If decay is evaluated lazily when a column is used, record the time needed to compute that decay; do not quietly forget a player effect simply because its chunk unloaded. This weather state is saved separately from frozen material state.

sections.title: Test the field without waiting for a storm
sections.html: The function should accept world position and integer world time as parameters. Use fixed neighbour values to test interpolation endpoints, midpoint and clamping. Then add deterministic baseline variation and compare repeated evaluations. A developer-only inspector can show baseline, delta and final value separately. That distinction makes it clear whether a sudden change came from seeded climate, a tool event or a bug in border interpolation.

47.outcome: Sheltered interiors stay dry, rain extinguishes fire within two seconds, and saturated surfaces create water without overwriting solids.
47.why: The rendered rain streak is an atmospheric cue. The simulation still needs a precise answer to “what did this rain hit?” The current design applies precipitation at exposed world surfaces, which avoids spawning a dense column of falling water blocks and prevents the camera height from changing travel time.

sections.title: Resolve the receiver in world coordinates
sections.html: For a column, the settled terrain heightmap gives the structural surface. Attached plants or burning material above that surface can be the actual precipitation receiver under the current rule. Query that receiver before applying water or snow. Do not use the top of the screen as a physical cloud or invent a hit inside an underground camera view. If the receiver lies outside the active region, the frozen-material policy prevents mutating it just because the weather baseline can be evaluated there.

sections.title: One hit has one accounted outcome
sections.html: A porous receiver absorbs until its capacity is reached. A saturated or nonporous receiver creates runoff in valid adjacent air according to the chosen placement rule; water must not overwrite stone or a roof. Plants absorb or drip under their own documented handling. A burning receiver first follows the extinguishing/wetting policy. Keep this as one simulation event so a decorative streak crossing the same column cannot apply another hit and double the rain rate.

sections.title: Choose rain versus snow from surface climate
sections.html: The snow decision belongs to ambient temperature at the world surface, not at the top of the current view. Otherwise panning upward could make the same hillside snow while panning down makes it rain. The exact threshold is part of the climate rule. The lab below uses temperature below zero for snow and nonnegative temperature for rain. For production, combine it with the actual weather field and light/medium/heavy hit probability.

sections.title: Build shelter fixtures before beautiful streaks
sections.html: Use one small scene with exposed soil, a roof over dry material, a leaf canopy, open water and an underground cavity. Apply the same scripted hits and assert which cells change. The roof receiver can become wet while the interior remains dry. Once those tests pass, draw streaks clipped at the same shelter boundary. If the visual treatment deliberately differs, label and approve that difference rather than allowing the renderer to silently choose a new simulation rule.

48.outcome: Wind is readable without material teleporting. Boundary tests distinguish gas removal from conserved mass stopping.
48.why: A single wind direction should influence smoke, snow and leaves without turning every material into the same substance. Boundary behavior makes this distinction important: smoke can disappear, steam contributes humidity, and conserved powders stop rather than vanish. We need material-aware outcomes at the active rectangle.

sections.title: Bias movement candidates, not coordinates blindly
sections.html: Wind can reorder or add horizontal candidates for a gas or light powder. Each candidate still needs an occupancy and path check. Adding a signed wind offset directly to an index can skip walls, go outside storage or move a cell twice. The simple rule should first attempt buoyant rise/fall as appropriate, then apply a bounded drift candidate. A deterministic strength or probability controls frequency without introducing frame-dependent random calls.

sections.title: Define boundary outcomes by kind
sections.html: The active margin is a simulation boundary, not the edge of the infinite world. A mass-bearing powder or liquid stays within it so the observer does not drain half a lake or lose drifting sand. Smoke is short-lived gas and is absorbed. Steam absorption adds humidity to its weather column. Ash is powder in the material table even though it visually accompanies smoke; do not accidentally route it through the gas-removal branch because its name sounds smoky.

sections.title: Move complete state and mark it once
sections.html: Temperature, moisture, lifetime and movement flags must travel with the material. The destination cannot receive a second update during a later scan or chunk phase. Wind often exposes these bugs because horizontal movement can enter an unvisited part of the same pass. Test a tagged parcel across a chunk edge and count how far it moved in one executed tick. The render loop must not independently drift the same smoke sprite and make physics and visuals disagree.

sections.title: Distinguish visual disappearance from accounting
sections.html: When steam leaves the active margin, the visual cell is removed but humidity receives a corresponding contribution according to the approximate water-cycle policy. Smoke may simply expire. A conserved powder remains in the last valid slot. Log separate counters during a fixture: absorbed smoke, credited steam, blocked powders. Then inspect the visible boundary while panning. Hidden removal at the margin does not prove there are no downstream physical effects; the policy is an accepted approximation that needs testing.

49.outcome: Small unsupported groups are identified correctly. The cap/off-region support exception is visible in tests and the acceptance requirement is scoped accordingly.
49.why: A floating row of two wooden cells can fool a local “solid beside me” test: each points to the other as support. We must ask about the connected structure as a whole. This is the first nonlocal search in the physics, so we also need a bound and a declared approximation.

sections.title: Define a group before looking for support
sections.html: Rigid cells connected by four-neighbour adjacency form one group. Collect that set using a queue or stack and a visited set. Only then can you distinguish internal contact from external support. Two cells in the collected group do not support each other against gravity; they are parts of one object. A proper anchor is bedrock or a valid supporting condition outside the group, as defined by the current game rules.

sections.title: Follow the queue in a tiny grid
sections.html: Begin with one affected rigid neighbour after a cell is removed. Pop it, skip if already visited, add its rigid neighbours, and continue. Mark visited when inserting or use a set on pop so loops cannot grow the work indefinitely. The lab below searches a one-dimensional chain to expose queue/visited behavior with minimal indexing. Port it to four-neighbour grid coordinates through your checked index helper, never raw unchecked arithmetic at edges.

sections.title: Bound the work and name the exception
sections.html: The design stops at 4096 cells or the active-region edge and treats the group as supported. This keeps a giant terrain mass from causing unbounded work, but it also makes some large floating structures remain airborne. That is not a proof of support; it is an accepted fallback if approved. Keep the result enum expressive: Supported, Unsupported, or AssumedSupportedBecauseLimit. Tests and developer counters should reveal which path was used instead of disguising it as an exact algorithm.

sections.title: Schedule searches only after relevant changes
sections.html: Removal of a rigid cell, a changed supporting cell, impact or an edit can dirty support. Queue affected starting positions and deduplicate them where useful. Running a full search from every cell every tick wastes work, while checking only player edits misses fire and erosion. After a blast, many events may refer to the same group. Bound the total support work per update and measure bursts, not merely the maximum size of one search.

50.outcome: A slab lands intact, a weak group breaks under the specified drop condition, and a raft/floe follows the approved buoyancy rule.
50.why: Once support identifies a loose roof piece, moving its cells independently would squash or stretch it. The structure needs one shared displacement. This is a useful change of representation: the world still contains cells, but a temporary group list describes a rigid motion decision across them.

sections.title: Test the whole move before writing any cell
sections.html: For every candidate downward displacement, inspect the destination of each member. Positions already occupied by the same group are not external collisions because they move together. Any external blocked destination rejects that displacement. Only after validating the complete candidate should cells be removed from old positions and placed in new positions. Interleaving validation and writes lets a partial group move while the remaining members collide with its own edits.

sections.title: Choose a shared path-limited displacement
sections.html: The design allows up to three rows per tick. Test displacements incrementally from one through three and keep the largest valid prefix. If an obstacle blocks row two, move one row rather than testing only row three and tunnelling through it. The same path logic applies to a group spanning chunks. Run this in the documented serial group pass, where one owner can inspect and apply the multi-chunk transaction without racing chunk workers.

sections.title: Float as a group under the approved rule
sections.html: Wood and ice are less dense than water in the material table, but a rigid aggregate may contain several materials. The current flotation rule needs an explicit group-density/support policy: minimum contact, displaced volume approximation or another declared simple test. Do not simply stop every solid above any liquid because stone would then float. Use small wooden raft, ice floe and metal/stone control fixtures and record the approximation before encoding it.

sections.title: Apply impact effects after landing
sections.html: Track travelled fall distance for the group so an impact can distinguish a short drop from a brittle break. The design’s weak-material threshold is more than eight cells. Landing first establishes the destination; breakup then converts or releases fragments according to their defined kinds. A group that reaches the active margin stops under the frozen boundary policy instead of deleting half its members. Tests should retain both shape offsets and per-material counts except for explicitly approved break/destruction rules.

51.outcome: No thrown material exists in both list and grid. Destruction beyond the cap is explicitly counted as the designed exception.
51.why: An explosion must throw matter outward, but ordinary grid cells only store material state, not a continuous velocity. A temporary particle list fills that gap. The key invariant is ownership: each thrown parcel is either in the grid or in the list, never both and never silently nowhere.

sections.title: Transfer ownership at launch
sections.html: When a blast chooses a cell for throwing, copy or move its complete state into a particle record, then clear its grid slot in the same event application. The record stores floating-point position and velocity plus original material/temperature/moisture fields needed on re-entry. A separate list has its own cap. If the cap is exhausted, the design destroys additional blast cells rather than spawning unlimited particles; count that exception so conservation tests know why matter disappeared.

sections.title: Integrate velocity using the physics tick
sections.html: Choose explicit units: position in cells and velocity in cells per physics second, or per tick. The worked lab uses seconds: position advances by velocity times dt and velocity by acceleration times dt. A fixed executed tick supplies dt, not the render frame duration. Interpolation between previous/current particle positions can make display motion smoother without changing the collision decision. This is a game effect, not a complete rigid-body physics engine.

sections.title: Sweep for collisions and bound reinsertion
sections.html: A fast particle can cross a wall between two endpoint samples. Trace the segment through candidate grid cells or otherwise sweep the path, stopping at the first non-gas hit. Reinsert the parcel into a nearby valid free slot using a bounded, deterministic search. “Nearest free” without a radius/order policy can become an unbounded flood fill or yield different answers across runs. A fully occupied region needs an explicit keep-pending/destruction/fallback policy rather than overwriting existing material.

sections.title: Treat saving as another ownership boundary
sections.html: The current design reinserts particles before saving, which changes a live explosion. That policy is still a design lab: either accept and demonstrate the visible interruption, or serialize particle state in a coherent snapshot. Do not claim exact mid-flight round trips while discarding velocity. The same ownership inventory should include falling groups and queued effects. A test that saves one tagged airborne parcel catches duplication or loss at this boundary more clearly than an entire blast cloud.

52.outcome: Gunpowder explodes within the one-second deadline and the explosion fixture shows a crater and outward motion. Destroyed material is counted as an explicit exception.
52.why: A particle engine does not create an explosion by itself. A charge needs an ignition/fuse trigger, one consumed event, a bounded selection of affected material, heat and outward motion. This lesson joins those pieces without leaving hot gunpowder as an infinite energy source.

sections.title: Turn ignition into one event
sections.html: When eligible gunpowder ignites, remove or mark the charge consumed and enqueue a Blast command with a world centre and declared strength/radius. Process it once in a deterministic event phase. A bomb fuse can enqueue the same command when it expires. Natural ignition and player tools therefore reuse the blast mechanism. If you simply test “hot gunpowder exists” every tick without consuming it, one charge detonates repeatedly and adds unlimited heat and destruction.

sections.title: Bound the affected coordinates first
sections.html: A circular blast of radius r only inspects the square from centre-r to centre+r, then accepts cells whose squared distance is at most r². Clip that rectangle to the active region and valid storage. Squared distance avoids a square root for selection, but its integer type must accommodate the maximum radius. The radius and strength caps are design/performance choices. Never let a malformed command or a giant brush request allocate an unbounded event list.

sections.title: Use hardness and ownership deliberately
sections.html: For each selected cell, decide whether it is untouched, destroyed or thrown based on the approved strength falloff and hardness rule. Thrown cells transfer into the particle list with outward velocity; destroyed cells are counted explicitly. The central cell needs a defined direction because normalizing a zero vector is invalid. Heat is another output of the blast and can trigger nearby fuel later. Keep these outcomes staged so a cell is not simultaneously thrown, destroyed and left in the grid.

sections.title: Test the required visible effects separately
sections.html: The one-second requirement applies to ignition and explosion effects at 1x. A fixture should assert the event is emitted once, a crater appears, material gains outward motion and nearby flammable matter receives heat/ignition under the selected rule. The flash and sound are readable decoration, not substitutes for a crater. At the particle cap, verify the designed destruction fallback rather than expecting strict mass conservation. A quiet closed fixture without destruction remains useful for ownership tests.

53.why: The lightning bolt is a drawing, but the strike is a world event. We must resolve what it hits before deciding heat or ignition. Otherwise an underground camera or a clipped bolt could change which cell receives the event.

sections.title: Resolve the world receiver
sections.html: The strike starts from the weather cloud-base concept and travels down to the first appropriate non-gas surface in its column. Use the existing world surface/exposure interface rather than scanning an infinite screen column. If the surface is outside active simulation, apply the explicitly chosen event policy instead of mutating frozen cells accidentally. A targeted lightning tool may select a cursor location under its own documented targeting rule, but natural lightning still resolves from weather and geometry.

sections.title: Separate material effects
sections.html: A flammable hit can ignite after the approved heat/ignition check. Metal conducts the strike through its connected group under the current design. That group search is not identical to support across arbitrary rigid materials: only the relevant conductive connectivity should participate. A metal roof beside stone should not heat every connected mountain cell merely because both belong to a rigid support group. Keep a conductivity/contact predicate for the event search.

sections.title: Bound an event that sounds instantaneous
sections.html: A “single bright frame” is a rendering duration, not permission for unlimited CPU work. A giant metal structure can span many chunks, so the conductive group operation needs the same kind of explicit cap/budget decision as support. Its order must not race normal cell phases. Queue the strike and apply the bounded effects serially or through owned outputs. A delayed thunder sound follows the event independently; it should not delay actual heat application.

Then move only the camera and repeat with an identical active interior. The same world receiver should be selected; only the visible portion of the bolt changes.

54.why: Painting Wood places material; selecting Lightning requests an event. The input bar needs to express that difference, while tests should be able to request the same event without a mouse. A command enum and explicit clock ownership make the tools small and reproducible.

sections.title: Convert input into commands
sections.html: Define commands such as Paint, Erase, Ignite, PlaceBomb, AddRain and Strike. The input layer maps cursor coordinates and selected page to one command; the simulation validates and executes it. UI hit testing happens first so clicking a tool swatch does not also paint behind the bar. Tests construct commands directly, which makes invalid targets and repeated presses easy to reproduce. Record command application tick and coordinates for later replay.

sections.title: Choose a clock for every duration
sections.html: The rain/lightning tool cooldown is one in-game day, so it reads world_tick. A three-second bomb fuse should name whether it measures physics ticks or calendar time; the course uses a physics-tick fuse as a proposed readable rule unless the milestone approves otherwise. At high fast-forward those clocks diverge. A duration stored as an unlabeled integer “60” is not enough: name the field next_ready_world_tick or fuse_steps_remaining so its units are visible in code.

sections.title: Store a deadline instead of decrementing every frame
sections.html: For cooldowns, compute ready_at = current_world_tick + duration once, then compare current time against it. This works across frame rate changes and does not require visiting every unavailable tool each render frame. Use checked or saturating arithmetic under the application’s long-run policy so an extreme counter does not wrap into immediate availability. Saving the deadline preserves cooldowns after load. A fuse tied to executed ticks remains separate and pauses with the simulation.

sections.title: Give rejected actions visible feedback
sections.html: An unavailable tool should not silently fire, reset its deadline or consume a charge. Return a small result such as Applied, CoolingDown(remaining) or InvalidTarget. The UI can show that result without owning the rule. Test exactly at ready_at as well as one tick before it. Repeated held input should obey the intended press/hold policy and not enqueue sixty charges per second merely because rendering repeats.

55.outcome: All M2 exit conditions are recorded with timings and a clip. Any oversized-group exception is stated rather than hidden.
55.why: Individual fire, rain and support tests are necessary, but the hillside scene is where their ordering becomes visible. A wet beam might burn if rain arrives after ignition; a roof may vanish from a stale support cache. This milestone assembles a small story while retaining enough instrumentation to diagnose it.

sections.title: Build one repeatable scene, not a random showcase
sections.html: Use a fixed hand-built hillside with a small house, dry grass, wet wood and a water basin. The M4 generator does not exist yet, so do not make this gate depend on generated lakes or biomes. Store fixture construction in code with a seed and initial climate context. The same scene can be used in tests, a manual play check and the episode recording. That shared fixture makes an observed problem easier to reproduce outside the video.

sections.title: Assert the sequence of causes and effects
sections.html: First dry grass catches and spreads under the chosen heat rule. Next scripted rain hits exposed fuel and stops the fire within two seconds. Wet wood resists ignition, the roof shelters its interior and a deliberately removed support makes a small floating roof fall. These are separate checks with first-observed timestamps. Do not treat a final screenshot of ash as evidence that all intermediate deadlines were met. Log enough state to distinguish ignition failure from material that already burned away.

sections.title: Include the moving observer
sections.html: Pan so a fire approaches the active margin, then return. The frozen policy stops off-region updates, but the visible frame should not contain an obviously stopped front under the accepted margin behavior. This manual check cannot prove unrestricted camera independence; it tests a scoped visual promise. Record camera positions and active rectangles so a regression can reproduce the same event. If the margin is insufficient, revise its measured cost and visibility tradeoff openly.

sections.title: Measure total event bursts
sections.html: An explosion may create particles, remove support, change heightmap entries and emit sound/visual events in one tick. Measure the complete synchronous tick and frame, including serial tails. A bounded 4096-cell fill repeated 100 times is still expensive. Record average and worst observed durations, event counts and resident memory with hardware/resolution. If the floor machine fails, reduce or redesign work before adding seasons, rather than relying on a later optimization miracle.

56.outcome: Day and season transitions are exact at their documented boundaries. Simulation step count is not silently substituted for calendar time.
56.why: We want a day to have an exact boundary, even when the computer cannot execute every desired physics update. One counter cannot represent both “updates actually performed” and “calendar time requested by fast-forward.” Two integer counters make that distinction visible and testable.

sections.title: Name what each counter counts
sections.html: step_tick increases once after a completed simulation update. It identifies update order and participates in deterministic random choices. world_tick advances by that update’s assigned multiplier and drives day, season, cooldowns and climate. At normal speed the increments are both one, which can hide the distinction. At fast-forward a single executed step may advance several calendar units. Give every timer a name tied to one of these clocks so a fuse cannot accidentally age like a season.

sections.title: Derive the calendar by division
sections.html: One day contains 24000 world ticks. Integer division yields the completed-day count and the remainder yields position within the day. Three days make a 72000-tick season; twelve days make a 288000-tick year. To display day one at startup, add one in the UI rather than changing the underlying zero-based counter. This avoids an off-by-one disagreement between calculations and labels. A calendar function can remain pure: it only reads the counter and returns derived fields.

sections.title: Test the boundaries, not only the middle
sections.html: Values just before, exactly at and just after 24000 or 72000 expose errors in division and modulo. A season can be represented as an enum selected by completed_seasons modulo four. The year count comes from division by 288000. Pausing freezes both advances under the current scheduler policy. Do not ask the OS date/time what season the simulated world is in; that would make saves and replays depend on when the game is launched.

sections.title: Plan for long-running storage
sections.html: u64 is large enough for ordinary play, but arithmetic should still have a declared overflow policy. Checked addition can surface a corrupted/extreme counter instead of wrapping the year backward. Save both counters because world_tick alone cannot reproduce which random picks occurred. Also decide how scheduler remainder/debt is persisted or reset; those are not the same as completed integer time. The lab isolates exact calendar conversion before scheduler budgeting is added in the next lessons.

57.outcome: Switching 64x to 1x leaves no physics backlog. Both measured frame work and uncancellable single-tick overshoots are reported honestly.
57.why: The first falling-cell clock taught elapsed time, but production must survive a slow tick, a dragged window and a speed change. The scheduler is a small policy engine: it decides which work is due, how much can run, and what debt is kept or discarded. We can test that policy without sleeping or opening a window.

sections.title: Separate real elapsed time from simulation time
sections.html: Measure wall-clock duration between frames, clamp it to the declared 250 ms maximum while unpaused, and accumulate it. Target tick period is 50 ms divided by selected speed. A paused frame contributes no elapsed time. Pause/speed changes reset the specified accumulators so old debt cannot create a burst after resuming. Inject elapsed values in a test rather than waiting for actual time; a test using sleeps is slower and subject to OS scheduling noise.

sections.title: Discard capped physics debt explicitly
sections.html: Compute how many target periods are due. Run no more than the measured count cap and frame-time policy allow, then keep only the sub-period fraction of physics elapsed time. Overdue whole physics updates do not remain queued. Their intended calendar advance is handled by world_tick_accum and multipliers, not by secretly catching up later. This distinction is what prevents a 64x-to-1x speed change from continuing to run a backlog of old physics work.

sections.title: A time budget is not a preemption mechanism
sections.html: The spec targets a single tick at most 10 ms and total simulation work at most 12 ms per rendered frame on the floor machine. Predict available work from measured tick cost before starting another synchronous update. Still measure afterward: a tick that unexpectedly takes 30 ms cannot be interrupted by a check performed after it completes. Report the overshoot honestly, adjust future work and investigate the slow rule. Do not claim that a post-tick if statement guarantees 60 FPS.

sections.title: Make planning pure before touching the live loop
sections.html: The lab below calculates a due count and retained fractional time only. Feed it known accumulated values and caps, including a long stall and cap zero. Production then combines that with pause, speed and predicted time budget. Keep tests for the actual early-stop path because k_plan and completed k can differ. Calendar debt remains owned by its accumulator until consumed by completed updates; the next lesson implements the allocation separately.

58.outcome: For every completed allocation, spent plus retained world ticks equals the accumulated budget. No early stop loses unspent calendar ticks.
58.why: Suppose the calendar owes ten ticks but only three physics updates fit. Assigning multiplier three to each loses one; assigning four to all creates two. Quotient and remainder give an exact integer distribution. Early stops then test whether the unspent time stays owned somewhere.

sections.title: Derive the allocation from a sum
sections.html: The invariant is simple: assigned calendar increments plus unspent calendar budget equals the initial whole budget. For W=10 and k=3, divide ten into three nearly equal integer pieces. The current spec repeatedly takes the ceiling of remaining W divided by remaining k, giving 4,3,3. This is not a new kind of fractional simulation tick; each completed physics update receives an integer multiplier. Fractional accepted calendar time stays in a separate fixed-point remainder.

sections.title: Avoid overflow in ceiling division
sections.html: A common formula (W+k-1)/k can overflow for very large W even when the final quotient fits. Compute W/k plus one when W%k is nonzero, or use a suitable integer div_ceil API supported by the pinned toolchain. Reject k=0 before dividing. In production W is selected so each planned update receives at least one; the helper below checks W>=k rather than silently inventing negative debt. All arithmetic choices need to match the actual accumulator representation.

sections.title: Spend only completed work
sections.html: If the first planned update gets four calendar ticks and then exceeds the frame budget, only those four are spent. Six remain in world_tick_accum. Do not pre-subtract the entire ten when planning three updates, because the remaining two may never run. A small allocation function can return a schedule for testing, while the live loop must commit each multiplier only after its update completes. Save/load or speed-reset policy must say what happens to unspent remainder.

sections.title: Keep exactness claims scoped
sections.html: The scheduler clamps long elapsed intervals and resets debt on pause/speed changes by design. Therefore exact conservation describes the accepted budget between those policy boundaries, not an unconditional promise to reproduce all external wall time. At high multipliers, calendar events and slow-process approximation can still differ from uncapped physics; exact sums do not make trajectories equivalent. Prove the arithmetic invariant separately from the visual/behavior tests at different speeds.

59.outcome: Off-screen cells receive no slow work. Fixed inputs reproduce the exact pick sequence, while measured frequencies are evaluated statistically.
59.why: Rot and growth do not need to scan every world cell on every physics tick. A bounded selection of active cells spreads work over time. To replay that selection, random choices must come from recorded inputs and sampling must not accidentally pick the same cell many times within one chunk tick.

sections.title: Build a permutation from an odd stride
sections.html: A chunk has 4096 cells, a power of two. Choose a start and an odd stride, then sample (start+i*stride) modulo 4096. Any odd stride is relatively prime to 4096, so the sequence visits every index before repeating. Taking its first 16 or at most 256 entries therefore gives distinct picks within that chunk tick. Derive start and stride from seed, executed tick and chunk position. The lab checks distinctness; choosing a good hash distribution is another documented implementation choice.

sections.title: Clip after sampling
sections.html: Boundary chunks overlap the active rectangle only partially. The design samples chunk-local indices, converts each into a world coordinate and skips picks outside the active region. This preserves the per-cell sampling opportunity under the specified procedure without updating frozen cells. Do not resample until you find 16 valid cells unless you intentionally change the rate at partially active edges. A fixed pick budget remains bounded even when only a tiny corner of a chunk is active.

sections.title: Understand expected visits, not guaranteed appointments
sections.html: At M=1, 16 picks times 20 executed ticks gives 320 picks per second per full chunk. Dividing 4096 by 320 gives 12.8 seconds between visits on average under an appropriately distributed changing permutation. Over a 24000-tick day that is 93.75 expected opportunities per cell. It is not a promise that every cell is visited at exact intervals. Use distributions across fixed seeds for rate tuning and precise fixed input sequences for regression.

sections.title: A parity bit is not enough for sparse visits
sections.html: The current spec proposes skipping a slow cell when its stored bit equals step_tick&1. A sparsely selected cell can retain that same bit from two ticks ago and be skipped even though it has not run this tick. Distinct picks solve duplicate selection, but created neighbour edits still need protection. Use a true last_updated_tick stamp in temporary active metadata or stage edits until the slow pass ends, then apply them in a fixed order. This is an explicit design correction to review, not a claim that the one-bit sparse guard is exact.

60.outcome: A cell cannot rot through two stages in one tick. Probability 0 stays 0 and probability 1 stays 1, including fallback mode.
60.why: Accelerated seasons should not reduce every cell to one huge irreversible jump. The revised design first increases the number of unit slow-work visits, then uses a capped approximation only when necessary. We need to preserve probability bounds and intermediate states while admitting where equivalence ends.

sections.title: Spend more picks before increasing step size
sections.html: For multiplier M, choose P=min(16*M,256). For M up to 16, each pick is an ordinary unit opportunity and the expected visit rate per world day remains aligned with normal mode, assuming the source distribution is appropriate. Above the cap, m=16*M/P describes represented unit opportunities per selected cell. The number of index attempts is bounded by overlapping chunks, not merely visible area; at the 720p active size chunk alignment can reach 35 overlapping chunks.

sections.title: Scale a chance through survival probability
sections.html: If one independent opportunity succeeds with probability p, surviving m opportunities without success is (1-p)^m. Therefore at least one success has chance 1-(1-p)^m. For integer m this is the familiar repeated-trial result; for fractional m the design uses its continuous survival extension. It stays within [0,1] for valid inputs, including exactly one when p=1. It does not represent the number of multiple possible events; the rule must define at most one event per allowed slow update.

sections.title: Preserve small rates and stage boundaries
sections.html: The spec floors m*rate before adding progress. If a small fractional rate is repeatedly rounded to zero, growth can stop forever. Choose fixed-point progress, a retained fractional remainder, or a documented stochastic rounding policy. Clamp the addition to the remaining distance to the next stage, not to a total cap added on top of already accumulated progress. When Wood reaches RottenWood, do not process the new stage again in the same simulation tick. Distinct picks plus staged edits/full tick stamps enforce that across neighbour creation too.

sections.title: Test the approximation, not a false equivalence
sections.html: At high m, spatial chains and multi-stage decay take at most one step per cell per executed tick. A tree cannot add its whole future canopy in one visit merely because many days were represented. That is a deliberate approximation and may produce different shapes at the same date under different hardware caps. Run fixed-seed and multi-seed fixtures at 1x,16x,64x including forced M=32; check acceptance outcomes and intermediate visibility, not exact world identity across unlike multiplier sequences.

61.outcome: A puddle dries faster than a lake. Moisture never leaves its allowed range, and seepage stops at nonporous material.
61.why: Rain and boiling were enough for short demonstrations, but an endless sandbox needs water to return and material to dry. Otherwise every rainy year either floods everything or every warm year deletes the lake. This lesson closes several small loops under a stated approximate regional budget.

sections.title: Distinguish stored water from wetness
sections.html: A Water cell is visible liquid occupancy. Moisture is stored state in porous material or the documented surface-wetness interpretation for metal. Absorption transfers an accounted rain/water portion into that state; saturation leaves later hits available for runoff. Because a full water cell and one moisture unit are not automatically equal, record the conversion scale and the approximate humidity policy. Tests should not claim exact atmospheric mass conservation when the model includes a noise-driven baseline and delta decay.

sections.title: Move seepage as a paired transfer
sections.html: For a wet porous upper cell and drier porous lower cell, transfer only up to the upper available content and lower remaining capacity. Apply equal-and-opposite amounts in the selected moisture units. A stone layer with zero capacity blocks this transfer. As with heat, choose whether the pass reads old state or staged deltas so scan order does not make one column drain arbitrarily faster. The lab computes a bounded pair transfer with integer values before the full lattice rule.

sections.title: Dry toward a context-defined equilibrium
sections.html: Exposed material loses moisture faster under warmth, sun and wind, while shelter greatly reduces that rate. Drying must not cross below zero or below the approved equilibrium target. A heat-drying step before ignition may generate steam; that path should not also count as ordinary atmospheric evaporation again. Separate the functions and event accounting enough to test them. A darker visual tint reads current moisture; it must not become a second hidden moisture state.

sections.title: Evaporate liquid through exposed surface cells
sections.html: Only exposed water with air above is eligible under the simple design. A shallow puddle has a large exposed fraction relative to its volume, so it can disappear sooner than a deep lake without a separate special puddle deletion rule. Credit weather humidity as specified, and let weather supply rain from that regional budget plus baseline. Use a hand-built pond for the year fixture before procedural lakes exist. Compare water levels over many seeds rather than tuning one lucky rainy run.

62.outcome: Wet fixtures visibly decay within their specified deadlines, dry controls do not, and intermediate states remain observable.
62.why: A wet hut should age visibly while a dry control remains sound. The game needs intermediate rotten wood and rust powder, not merely a timer that deletes every old structure. We already have slow-work opportunities; now we connect them to conditional progress and explicit material transitions.

sections.title: Progress is conditional history
sections.html: A slow visit should first check the material’s current qualifying condition, such as moisture above a threshold. If it qualifies, increase progress using the chosen fixed-point/integer rate; otherwise apply the approved stop/recovery rule. Decide whether dry periods pause or reverse accumulated rot. The spec establishes wetness dependence but not every recovery coefficient, so record that tuning decision rather than invent a universal physical law. A dry control catches accidental unconditional aging.

sections.title: Cross one stage at a time
sections.html: Wood reaches a rot threshold and becomes RottenWood. That new material has different hardness/support consequences and later crumbles into Soil. Metal reaches its threshold and becomes Rust powder, which can fall or wash away. Reset or reinterpret progress at each material transition and prevent another slow transition in the same executed tick. A stage cap must account for current progress so an addition cannot overshoot or wrap the u8. Distinct sample picks do not by themselves protect newly modified neighbours.

sections.title: Read the correct wetness state
sections.html: Metal has zero porosity in the material properties, so rust must use the approved surface-wetness path from the earlier lab. The same field can be interpreted per material only if conversion rules are clear. For wood, absorbed moisture and heat drying influence ignition as well as rot. Place wet and dry beams in matching environments and record moisture alongside progress. Otherwise a failed rot test may actually be a drying or initialization bug.

sections.title: Verify visible states and structural consequences
sections.html: A test that skips directly to final Soil does not show that RottenWood was ever observable. Record first entry into each stage and retain the intermediate state for at least the allowed slow-update timing. Rotten wood should weaken support/impact according to the material rule rather than preserve normal wood hardness. Rust removes whole metal cells under this grid model, so a sheet becomes thinner by losing outer cells, not through subpixel geometry. Review the actual four-pixel rendering as well as state counts.

63.outcome: Channels become visible at the required deadline while the hill retains its broad shape over the longer fixture.
63.why: Rain should carve a channel, but the same rule repeated for years should not erase every hillside. Erosion is a spatial transfer with two time-scale promises: enough change to notice soon, and enough stability to keep a recognizable world later. Both must guide tuning.

sections.title: Move material rather than simply deleting it
sections.html: An eligible exposed loose cell checks a downhill destination and moves there under the bounded rule. That transfer changes the surface heightmap at source and destination. In a closed fixture, the number of Soil/Sand/Ash/Rust cells should remain constant unless a separately specified conversion occurs. Deleting the source and never depositing it can create a convincing channel in a screenshot while silently draining the landscape. The test should count matter as well as shape change.

sections.title: Define eligibility and direction explicitly
sections.html: The design uses sky exposure, slope and rain or soaked-from-rain state. Derive slope from neighbouring settled surface heights rather than from screen shading. Tie-break left and right deterministically. Keep a local move bound and validate the entire path so erosion does not tunnel through a stone dam. Stone erodes at a much smaller rate and may need its own threshold/progress policy. Do not reuse rapid sand falling as the erosion rate; they solve different timescales.

sections.title: Stage neighbouring edits carefully
sections.html: Two sampled cells may select the same destination. Use a fixed deterministic application order or reserve targets in a staged edit pass. If a source moves downhill into a later selected cell, the once-per-tick guard should keep it from eroding twice. Update exposure metadata after committed changes, not from an intermediate half-edited world that another worker can read unpredictably. This is a good reason to keep slow erosion edits serial or staged while the basic rule is being established.

sections.title: Tune with short and long fixtures
sections.html: Measure a bare-soil slope under scripted rain for one in-game day at 16x and record a channel profile. Then run many years under the declared weather schedule and compare broad crest/slope metrics. A channel can deepen locally while the overall hill retains its shape. The exact acceptable metrics are a design decision, but they must be written before judging the result. Use a dry control and a stone-rich control so the test can distinguish erosion from gravity instability in generated terrain.

64.outcome: The isolated fixture either recovers under the approved rule or exposes a decision still needed. The seasonal recovery requirement is not claimed from neighbour spread alone.
64.why: A completely burned patch has no living grass neighbour. A neighbour-spread rule cannot recover it, no matter how many times we run the loop. That is a missing prerequisite, not a rate-tuning problem. We need to decide what survives or arrives after fire before promising recovery.

sections.title: Trace the dependency of ordinary spread
sections.html: The simple rule asks for Soil, sufficient light and moisture, and a nearby living Grass source. When all four exist, one eligible visit may replace a target with Grass. The newly created cell must not immediately spread again later in the same tick. This local rule is attractive because its cause is readable: green edges creep into bare soil. But it cannot manufacture its own starting source in a sealed all-burned fixture.

sections.title: Choose one minimal recovery mechanism
sections.html: Options include surviving roots stored with soil, a bounded seed bank, rare seed arrival from the environment, or scoping the requirement to patches connected to surviving grass. Each changes behavior and storage. For this design lab, propose a boolean dormant-root condition that allows regrowth on exposed moist soil after fire. This is a teaching proposal, not an already approved material field. Compare its cost and player readability to a seed-source alternative before altering the packed Cell layout.

sections.title: Integrate death as well as growth
sections.html: Grass buried under settled material loses light and eventually returns to soil under the current design. Fire can consume Grass into Ash, while leaves/ash on soil contribute soil formation. Regrowth should not appear through an intact stone floor or inside a dark cave merely because the seed/root condition exists. Put environment checks around the recovery source. A root mechanism may survive burning but not arbitrary erasure; decide and test those distinctions instead of allowing invisible immortal grass everywhere.

sections.title: Use the impossible case as the central test
sections.html: Build a small isolated bare-soil island with no adjacent Grass. Under neighbour-only spread it should remain bare; that control proves the test is truly isolated. Enable the proposed root/seed source and run moist lit conditions through the seasonal deadline. Add dry and buried controls that must not recover. This demonstrates why the new mechanism is necessary and prevents “fixing” the requirement by accidentally leaving one hidden Grass cell in the fixture.

65.outcome: A growing tree never overwrites a house. Detached leaves drift and eventually join the soil-formation cycle.
65.why: Trees must be built from the same wood and leaf cells as everything else. Otherwise fire, support and a player’s brush cannot affect them consistently. A template supplies a simple growth direction while collision checks keep the living world from painting over a newly built house.

sections.title: Represent a template as relative offsets
sections.html: Store a small list of offsets from a sapling origin, each with a material to add. Trunk steps come before supported branch/leaf steps under the chosen template. A growth stage identifies the next candidate rather than allocating a complete invisible tree. The template is data, so an evergreen pine and a deciduous tree can share the growth mechanism while choosing different cells and leaf-cycle behavior. Avoid starting with a procedural branching research project when a few authored templates can prove the ecological loop.

sections.title: Validate every addition at the moment of growth
sections.html: The world may change after the sapling appears. Before adding each cell, check target occupancy, active-region policy, attachment/support and any maximum height/density constraints. An empty space at planting time is not permission to overwrite a roof ten days later. If blocked, choose a declared policy: pause the stage, abandon that branch, or try an approved alternate. Keep it deterministic and bounded. The lab demonstrates a reservation-like check with a boolean occupancy buffer.

sections.title: Track living attachment without circular immortality
sections.html: Rooted trunk wood and attached leaves stay in place; detached leaves become light powder. A local leaf-to-leaf rule can leave a floating loop that claims mutual attachment, much like the old support bug. Define living connectivity to an actual trunk/root source, using bounded search or maintained tree metadata as approved. Autumn detaches deciduous leaves; evergreen needles remain. Spring regrowth depends on a living tree source, not merely any leaf-coloured cell nearby.

sections.title: Keep growth and leaf cycles within slow-work bounds
sections.html: A high calendar multiplier must not instantiate a whole tree in one unbounded operation. Advance at most the allowed stage/cell per executed tick and guard newly created targets from immediate further growth. Leaf litter eventually contributes soil formation under moisture/soil-contact rules, closing renewal with decay. Measure dense forests later; one template is cheap, but thousands of plants competing for targets and connectivity checks can change worst-case tick cost.
