66.outcome: Season boundaries align with the integer clock. Visual side effects of accelerated climate are documented and tested.
66.why: A season is not only a label in the HUD. It changes sky colour, ambient temperature and ecological rates, while local matter responds through its own tick-based rules. Connecting those layers gives the calm world its rhythm, but it also exposes the deliberate difference between calendar speed and physical response.

sections.title: Derive presentation from a single calendar
sections.html: Use world_tick for time of day and seasonal position, then evaluate sky keys, sun path and climate parameters from that value. Do not let the renderer maintain a separate drifting day timer. A paused world should hold its sky and season. The night/dusk/day colours come from approved art keys; missing transition colours and moon-phase paths are visual decisions to approve. Interpolation should move coherently between those keys without randomly tinting neighbouring cells differently.

sections.title: Keep ambient as a world function
sections.html: Ambient depends on season, time of day, weather-column offset and altitude relative to sea level. Evaluate it for the relevant cell or receiver, never the view’s top row. Sky-exposed and air-exposed conditions still have separate roles. Sheltered air uses the chosen season-mean policy instead of the full day/night swing. A basement can therefore remain more stable than an exposed puddle. This is a deliberately cheap game model, not a fluid simulation of air circulation.

sections.title: Let material respond through heat and moisture rules
sections.html: Changing the season should not directly replace every Water cell with Ice or set all wood to dry. The ambient target changes, then exposure and heat exchange move cell temperatures; slow drying/growth opportunities use the new environmental context. This preserves causal links: shallow water freezes from its surface and sheltered wood can retain moisture. Use a fixture with exposed and sheltered copies so a direct global overwrite becomes obvious.

sections.title: Name the high-speed mismatch
sections.html: At a large multiplier, the sky and ambient target can advance many calendar units while only one physical heat/movement update occurs. A winter may arrive before a deep lake has had normal-speed-equivalent cooling. That is an accepted fast-forward approximation if its visual outcome meets the milestone requirements. Record multiplier sequences and compare visible results at 1x,16x,64x. Exact calendar arithmetic does not establish identical physical states at the same date; avoid promising that in the episode narration.

67.outcome: All required seeds pass or failures become tracked design work. Lake level stays within the specified 20 percent bound in the acceptance fixture.
67.why: A single wet beam can pass its test while the whole world still ends a year as a lifeless dry basin. The ecology milestone needs both narrow fixtures and a long-run scene. It also needs evidence across seeds, because random opportunities can make one demonstration look healthier than the underlying rule.

sections.title: Separate regression and reliability questions
sections.html: A fixed regression seed recreates a known failure exactly. The 32-seed reliability suite asks whether each accepted scenario succeeds across a documented set of distinct sequences. Both are deterministic tests when the seeds and multiplier histories are fixed. Neither makes randomness disappear; they provide repeatable evidence over chosen cases. Do not keep changing seeds until a flaky assertion turns green, and do not claim mathematical certainty from a finite sample.

sections.title: Use crafted terrain before the generator exists
sections.html: M3 comes before M4 procedural generation. Build the plains-and-lake fixture directly with a known bowl, saturated underlying soil, stable slopes, grass/tree sources and climate inputs. Store the fixture parameters in code and reuse them in the episode scene. This prevents a later generator dependency from blocking ecological work and makes any water-level change easier to attribute. A handcrafted scene is valid evidence for the scoped M3 gate, not proof that every future generated lake is stable.

sections.title: Measure multiple outputs at the end
sections.html: The design requires grass, trees and water remaining, plus lake level within 20 percent of its start in the acceptance fixture. Measure water volume and surface height carefully: a one-cell surface shift can have different volume meaning depending on bowl shape. Record starting and final values using the agreed metric, vegetation counts and any cap/overload events. A screenshot of one surviving green pixel is not sufficient evidence that the ecological loop is healthy and readable.

sections.title: Make failure diagnostic rather than merely red
sections.html: When a seed fails, report which condition failed, first divergence time if available, climate history, step/world tick counts and water-accounting totals. The cause may be absent regrowth sources, evaporation scale, a frozen-region test boundary or stage-skipping under high multipliers. Keep the smallest failing seed/fixture as regression. Then rerun the full reliability set only after a rule change, preserving the original case so the fix cannot hide a new failure elsewhere.

68.outcome: The same world cell can be drawn and picked after panning. Increasing altitude moves it upward, not downward.
68.why: The early renderer counted rows downward from the top-left corner. The world design counts altitude upward. Both conventions are valid, but silently using one where the other is expected reverses gravity, growth and camera picking. One named conversion makes the relationship explicit.

sections.title: Name spaces before writing formulas
sections.html: World coordinates describe persistent locations independent of the current view. Camera coordinates describe which world area appears in the window. Drawing coordinates are measured downward/rightward from the view origin. Local chunk coordinates are offsets inside one 64×64 storage block. These are related spaces, not interchangeable integers. Separate types are useful when practical; at minimum use names such as world_y, view_top_y and screen_row rather than a generic y everywhere.

sections.title: Derive the vertical conversion
sections.html: If the top visible world altitude is top_y, a cell at altitude y appears top_y-y rows down. A world altitude increase makes the result smaller, so the cell moves upward on the screen. Multiply that row by the drawing cell size only after this conversion. For x, subtract the camera’s left world x. The inverse adds the horizontal offset and subtracts the screen row from top_y. Decide whether camera origins are cell-aligned or rounded at drawing boundaries and test the chosen picking behavior.

sections.title: Keep physics in world units
sections.html: After adopting world altitude, falling decreases world y, rising steam increases it and a trunk template grows with positive y offsets. Do not change the physical rule based on screen orientation; only the renderer/picking conversion knows about downward rows. When porting prototype code, search every row+1 gravity operation and classify whether it belongs to a screen grid or world state. Rename deliberately instead of flipping signs blindly across all expressions.

sections.title: Negative coordinates need Euclidean chunk mapping
sections.html: For world x=-1 and chunk width 64, the containing chunk is -1 and local offset is 63. Truncating division would point at chunk zero with an invalid negative local position. Use div_euclid and rem_euclid so reconstruction chunk*64+local returns the original coordinate. Test -65,-64,-1,0,63,64. A viewport that crosses the origin should neither mirror cells nor lose brush strokes.

69.outcome: Shared borders match and generation order does not alter terrain. Seed and generator-version inputs are explicit.
69.why: Exploration should reveal the same hillside regardless of the route taken to reach it. A single mutable RNG consumed while loading chunks makes terrain depend on visit order. A coordinate-addressed height function instead lets any chunk ask for its columns independently.

sections.title: Define the generation key
sections.html: Terrain generation takes world seed, generator version and world coordinate. It returns the same result for that tuple. The version is as important as the seed because changing a formula changes absent chunks in an old save. Begin with a simple one-dimensional height function before adding caves and climate. This keeps the first border test small: evaluate adjacent columns directly and compare them with the values embedded in separately generated chunks.

sections.title: Make broad variation continuous
sections.html: Independent random heights at every column create white-noise spikes rather than calm hills. Sample a deterministic value at widely spaced lattice points, then blend between them. A smoothstep blend eases the slope near endpoints. Add a lower-amplitude, shorter-scale component only after broad shape works. The lab uses a tiny deterministic hash and one smooth scale to show the mechanism; it is not a recommendation that this particular hash is the final generator’s quality choice.

sections.title: Treat negative positions as ordinary world coordinates
sections.html: Find the lattice interval with Euclidean division and a nonnegative remainder. That makes x=-1 blend between the correct lattice centres instead of joining the wrong interval at zero. Coordinate hashing should use explicitly chosen wrapping integer operations, so debug builds and release builds do not differ because of overflow checks. Do not use the standard randomized hash-map hasher as an unspecified persistent terrain generator. Pin the algorithm/configuration if worlds must regenerate across versions.

sections.title: Test order independence and borders
sections.html: Generate chunk A then B, record their heights, then generate B then A in a fresh world. The values should match because no mutable visit sequence is consumed. Check the exact shared boundary and a run across negative coordinates. Later rest guarantees may modify material placement based on slopes, but should still be deterministic functions of bounded neighbourhood data. A beautiful random-looking picture is not evidence that regeneration or old-world compatibility works.

70.outcome: Biome borders have no chunk seams. Starting terrain largely remains still under the rest test.
70.why: A height function draws a hill, but the simulation decides whether that hill can stand. Putting loose soil on every steep face creates a world that collapses as soon as it enters view. Biomes and strata must therefore generate material arrangements compatible with the rules we already taught.

sections.title: Choose context before material layers
sections.html: A slowly varying biome field chooses plains, mountain, sea or beach context per world column. It should form broad regions rather than alternate every few cells. Base height and biome may use separate keyed noise inputs so changing a biome decision does not accidentally scramble the entire height sequence. Blend parameters where appropriate, but material identity remains discrete: a transition band can choose a coherent boundary rather than invent an unsupported half-sand half-stone substance.

sections.title: Compute slope from neighbouring heights
sections.html: For each column, inspect a bounded neighbourhood of settled surface heights. Compare steepness with the material’s approved repose constraint. A low-slope plains column can carry soil, while a steep mountain face exposes stone. Use the same inequality convention as the powder-rest rule, including equality. If generation permits a slope that motion considers unstable, every newly active chunk will rearrange. The lab below makes this consistency decision explicit with a simple maximum height-step threshold.

sections.title: Place strata in a defined order
sections.html: The current design uses soil over stone, with sand at beaches/dunes. Depth can vary deterministically with a low-amplitude field. Water placement and later features must respect the base solid geometry; unsupported boulders, caves immediately below the sea or dry soil under generated water can break the rest guarantee even when slopes look correct. Build generation as ordered functions with explicit inputs and inspect a cross-section before adding every feature. Material colours should communicate strata without speckled per-cell noise.

sections.title: Verify rest before polishing biomes
sections.html: Generate a sample set spanning all v1 biomes and run 600 ordinary simulation ticks. The milestone allows fewer than 0.1 percent of cells to move in the rest fixture. Count actual moved cells or an agreed displacement metric, not only final-state difference, because a grain could move and later return. Use the same generator version and environment inputs for reproducibility. If the scene is unstable, fix generation or reconcile the movement constraints before hiding it under atmospheric art.
